results.title: What is a sysroot? - Quora
results.content: A sysroot is a directory tree that contains a minimal, self-consistent set of system headers, libraries, and runtime files used by a compiler, linker and toolchain to build and link programs for a specific target environment. It isolates the target’s system files from the host system so cross-compilation or controlled builds use the intended ABI, headers, and library versions. A sysroot is a directory tree that contains a minimal, self-consistent set of system headers, libraries, and runtime files used by a compiler, linker and toolchain to build and link programs for a specific target environment. It isolates the target’s system files from the host system so cross-compilation or controlled builds use the intended ABI, headers, and library versions. A sysroot is a controlled filesystem tree that supplies the headers and libraries a compiler and linker use to build for a target environment, essential for cross-compilation and reproducible, isolated builds. To build a sysroot, create a directory and copy into it the executables, libraries and configuration files that you need. Normally the next step would be a pivot\_root operation to switch `/sysroot` into a real root filesystem, start executing stuff from there and then remove the initramfs from memory. The `chroot /sysroot` command means: "start a new shell in such a way that for that shell the `/sysroot` directory will appear as `/`." Within that chrooted shell, `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/shadow` will refer to the real password files in the real root filesystem, and `/bin/passwd` will be the same command you'll use when the system is running normally.

results.title: How to cross compile with LLVM based tools
results.content: ● We want to use as much of the LLVM libraries as possible ○ compiler-rt ○ libc++, libc++abi, libunwind Building and running the application prompt$ root=/path/to/clang/install_dir prompt$ sysroot=/path/to/linarogcc/aarch64-linux-gnu/libc prompt$ ${root}/bin/clang++ --target=aarch64-linux-gnu -fsanitize=undefined \ --rtlib=compiler-rt --stdlib=libc++ \ -nostdinc++ -I${root}/include/c++/v1 \ -Wl,-L${root}/lib \ --sysroot ${sysroot} \ --gcc-toolchain=/path/to/linarogcc \ -rpath ${root}/lib \ example.cpp -o example prompt$ qemu-aarch64 -L ${sysroot} example Hello World example.cpp:16:7: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int' Cross compiling the LLVM libraries yourself ● The home pages for the libraries have build instructions for standalone builds. ● You can use clang option --print-search-dirs to see effect of options ○ For example --target, --sysroot, --gcc-toolchain Conclusions ● Clang can work well as a cross-compiler for a Linux environment if you have a cross compiling gcc installation available.

results.title: makefile - Cross compiling and sysroot - Raspberry Pi Stack Exchange
results.content: # Cross compiling and sysroot. I've been following instructions to cross compile code for the Raspberry Pi but I need some clarification regarding the tool chain and sysroot. Within rpi-cross I created a sysroot directory and then used rsync to copy files from the target. export CROSS_COMPILE=/home/j/rpi-cross/tools/arm-bcm2708/arm-linux-gnueabihf/bin/arm-linux-gnueabihf- export SYSROOT=/home/j/rpi-cross/sysroot. CC=$(CROSS_COMPILE)gcc hello-world : main.c $(CC) --sysroot=$(SYSROOT) -march=armv6 -mfpu=vfp -mfloat-abi=hard -o hello-world main.c. But I got the following output:. In file included from main.c:1:0: /home/j/rpi-cross/sysroot/usr/include/stdio.h:27:36: fatal error: bits/libc-header-start.h: No such file or directory #include. /home/j/rpi-cross/tools/arm-bcm2708/arm-rpi-4.9.3-linux-gnueabihf/bin/../lib/gcc/arm-linux-gnueabihf/4.9.3/../../../../arm-linux-gnueabihf/bin/ld: cannot find crt1.o: No such file or directory /home/j/rpi-cross/tools/arm-bcm2708/arm-rpi-4.9.3-linux-gnueabihf/bin/../lib/gcc/arm-linux-gnueabihf/4.9.3/../../../../arm-linux-gnueabihf/bin/ld: cannot find crti.o: No such file or directory. I then edited the makefile as follows, removing the sysroot option, and put the call to printf back into main.c. CC=$(CROSS_COMPILE)gcc hello-world : main.c $(CC) -march=armv6 -mfpu=vfp -mfloat-abi=hard -o hello-world main.c. At which point the build was succesful and after copying the application onto the target I was able to run it. Further investigation reveals that there is a sysroot folder under `/home/james/rpi-cross/tools/arm-bcm2708/arm-rpi-4.9.3-linux-gnueabihf/arm-linux-gnueabihf/` which I assume the toolchain uses by default. This brings me to the crux of the question; what is wrong with the sysroot that I created by copying files from my target device? * I used the above solution with RPI-5 CROSS\_COMPILE = aarch64-linux-gnu- CC = $(CROSS\_COMPILE)gcc hello-world: main.c $(CC) --sysroot=$(SYSROOT) -o hello-world main.c # Fixed command clean: rm -f hello-world and it worked. # Define our host system SET(CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME Linux) set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR arm) # Define the cross compiler locations set(tools /home/david/raspi/tools/arm-bcm2708/gcc-linaro-arm-linux-gnueabihf-raspbian-x64) set(CMAKE_C_COMPILER ${tools}/bin/arm-linux-gnueabihf-gcc) set(CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER ${tools}/bin/arm-linux-gnueabihf-g++) set(CMAKE_STAGING_PREFIX /home/david/stage) # Don't mess with the sysroot, despite every post saying you should #set(CMAKE_SYSROOT ${tools}/arm-linux-gnueabihf) # Use our definitions for compiler tools SET(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_PROGRAM NEVER) # Search for libraries and headers in the target directories only SET(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_LIBRARY ONLY) SET(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_INCLUDE ONLY) set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_PACKAGE ONLY).
